captions: Welcome to Atomic Education.
This lesson was created by Atomic Education to help you learn Cambridge Lower Secondary Science with confidence. Let's begin!
Welcome to Unit 14: Planetary Systems.

The Universe is everything: all of space, time, matter and energy. Looking at the night sky, you see cosmic history, because starlight takes years to reach us. But light pollution is hiding the stars.

On a truly dark night, you can see the Milky Way, our home galaxy. It's a spiral galaxy, like a giant spinning pinwheel, containing hundreds of billions of stars. Our Sun is on one of its spiral arms, about 27 thousand light years from the centre.

The Milky Way is one of trillions of galaxies. It belongs to a Local Group of about 54 galaxies held together by gravity. Our closest major neighbour, Andromeda, is heading our way, but it will take about four billion years to arrive!

Galaxies come in different shapes. Spiral galaxies like ours have arms. Elliptical galaxies are oval, like rugby balls. Lenticular galaxies are lens-shaped with a bulge in the middle. Irregular galaxies have no defined shape.

A galaxy contains stars, planetary systems, gas and clouds of stellar dust: tiny specks of ice, carbon, silicon, oxygen and metals. Unlike house dust, it isn't skin and hair! It blocks our view, but it's the building block of new planetary systems.
The Universe is also expanding. Imagine galaxies as dots on a balloon being blown up: they all move further and further apart.

captions: A planetary system is one star and all the objects held in orbit around it by gravity: planets, moons, comets, asteroids and tiny bits of ice and rock. Ours is the Solar System, with the Sun at its centre.
Eight planets orbit the Sun in elliptical paths. Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars are rocky planets; Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune are gas planets. All except Mercury and Venus have moons.

Planets and moons are non-luminous: we see them because they reflect sunlight. That's why stars twinkle but planets shine with a steady light. Astronomers have found over four thousand other stars with planets, called exoplanets.

About 4.6 billion years ago, the Solar System formed from a nebula: a giant cloud of gas and stellar dust. Gravity pulled it inwards and it began to spin, forming a hot protostar at the centre, which became the Sun.

Around it, dust and rock stuck together into protoplanets, which grew into planets. Rocks left over became asteroids. Most orbit between Mars and Jupiter, in the asteroid belt, where Jupiter's strong gravity stopped them forming a planet.

Dwarf planets are bigger than asteroids but smaller than planets, and gravity has rounded their shape. Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006. Beyond Neptune lies the Kuiper Belt, full of icy objects.

Comets are made of ice, dust and rock and follow very long, thin orbits. Near the Sun, the ice turns to gas, releasing dust that the Sun's radiation pushes into a tail. So a comet's tail always points away from the Sun.

captions: Earth has a solid inner core and a liquid outer core of molten iron and nickel. This molten metal is always moving, creating electric currents that produce a magnetic field. So Earth's core acts like a giant magnet, with a field reaching far into space.

The magnetic North pole isn't at the geographic pole, and it wanders about 10 kilometres a year. The field deflects the solar wind, charged particles from the Sun that could strip away our atmosphere and harm life.

The solar wind also creates beautiful auroras, the northern and southern lights, when its particles collide with atoms in the atmosphere and give out light. And spacecraft can use solar sails, pushed by the solar wind, to travel through space.
Now it is your turn to shine! Pause the video after each question and try to answer it first.
Question 1: What is the Milky Way? Pause the video now.
Answer: A spiral galaxy of billions of stars, including the Sun.
Question 2: Name the four shapes of galaxies. Pause the video now.
Answer: Spiral, elliptical, lenticular and irregular.
Question 3: Why does a comet's tail point away from the Sun? Pause the video now.
Answer: The Sun's radiation pushes the dust away.
Question 4: What causes Earth's magnetic field? Pause the video now.
Answer: Moving molten iron and nickel in the outer core.
